newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia sets NATO, presidential poll referendums.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia sets NATO, presidential poll referendums.

text.p: Slovak President Michal Kovac, in a bid to outflank Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, on Thursday named the day for a referendum on a constitutional change to allow direct presidential elections.
Slovaks will be asked to vote on May 23 and 24 on the proposed change, which is bitterly opposed by Meciar, once a supporter and ally of the president but now an avowed foe.
Kovac said a referendum on whether Slovakia should join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) would be held at the same time.
"I shall launch a personal campaign before the two referenda and will advocate a 'yes' vote to both," Kovac said after announcing the plebiscite.
The referendum is a direct challenge to Meciar, whose ruling three-party coalition defeated an opposition attempt in parliament to change the constitution in favour of direct presidential elections.
The opposition then collected the 350,000 signatures needed to force the issue to a referendum.
"Those who signed the petition were duped because this was no agreement in parliament but a demonstrative action," Meciar said.
Kovac's term of office expires next March, while elections to a new parliament, which would elect a president under the present constitution, will not be held until the following autumn.

The coalition, led by Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), and the opposition appear unable to agree on a presidential candidate. Neither commands the three-fifths majority needed to push through its own choice in the March 1998 vote.

In the event of such a stalemate, Meciar would assume presidential powers until a new parliament were elected in general elections in September or October. The referendum is seen as an attempt to deny Meciar the presidency.

Meciar has made several unsuccessful attempts to oust Kovac but has failed because of insufficient support in parliament. But he has managed to whittle down the president's powers, continually slashing the presidential office budget.
Kovac had no choice but to call both referendums. The opposition collected some 500,000 signatures for the vote on elections and parliament approved the NATO ballot.

Slovakia, created after Czechoslovakia split in 1993, is keen to be among the first new members of NATO, but its chances are believed to have waned after Western criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
"It is the duty of all concerned who have it in their political programmes to convince the population of the need to vote in favour of NATO membership," Kovac said.

He said Slovakia's hopes of being invited to start membership negotiations at the NATO summit in Madrid in July were slim, but a 'yes' vote in the referendum would help those backing Slovakian membership.
The opposition has charged that the questions are deliberately phrased to make people vote against membership.
A public opinion poll in December showed only 35.1 percent of Slovaks supported NATO membership and 25.5 percent opposed it.
